Emergency Kit for UK Motorcycle Touring

No one plans for an emergency, but every smart tourer prepares for one. The remoteness that makes British motorcycle touring so magical is the same remoteness that makes emergencies serious. A well-assembled emergency kit weighs under 1kg and could genuinely save your life or someone else's.

First Aid Kit

A motorcycle-specific first aid kit should handle the injuries most likely in a riding incident:

  • Trauma dressings: Large sterile pads for wound coverage. More useful than a box of plasters.
  • Conforming bandages: For securing dressings and supporting sprains.
  • Triangular bandage: Works as a sling, tourniquet, or head bandage.
  • Adhesive wound closures (Steri-Strips): For closing minor cuts without stitches.
  • Antiseptic wipes: For cleaning wounds before dressing.
  • Latex-free gloves: Two pairs minimum. Always use gloves when treating bleeding.
  • Scissors and tweezers: Small trauma scissors for cutting clothing or bandages.
  • Painkillers: Paracetamol and ibuprofen.
  • Antihistamines: For insect bites and allergic reactions.

Survival Essentials

  • Emergency bivvy bag: A reflective survival bag weighing under 100g. If you're stranded overnight in the Highlands in cold weather, this could save your life by retaining body heat.
  • Emergency whistle: Carries further than shouting and requires less energy. Six blasts is the universal mountain distress signal.
  • Head torch: Hands-free light for roadside repairs, camp setup, or signalling. Keep spare batteries.
  • Fire-starting kit: Waterproof matches or a lighter. Useful for warmth, signalling, and morale.
  • High-visibility vest: Legally required in some European countries and extremely useful if you break down at dusk on a rural road.

Communication and Location

  • Fully charged phone: Your primary emergency tool. Save ICE (In Case of Emergency) contacts.
  • What3Words app: Gives emergency services your exact location even where there's no address or postcode.
  • Written emergency information: In your jacket pocket, keep a card with your name, blood type, emergency contact, medical conditions, and allergies. If you're unconscious, this helps paramedics.
  • Power bank: A charged power bank ensures your phone works when you need it most.
The What3Words app is used by every UK emergency service. Download it, learn how it works, and you can give a precise location from anywhere. It works offline with GPS. In a genuine emergency in rural Britain, it's invaluable.

What to Do in an Emergency

If you're involved in or come across an accident:

  • Scene safety first: Ensure the scene is safe before approaching. Move bikes and people off the road if possible.
  • Call 999: Give your location (What3Words or road name), number of casualties, and type of injuries. Stay on the line.
  • Don't remove helmets: Unless the casualty isn't breathing. Helmet removal by untrained people can cause spinal injury.
  • Control bleeding: Apply direct pressure with a sterile dressing. Elevate the limb if possible.
  • Keep the casualty warm: Shock causes rapid heat loss. Use your emergency bivvy bag, spare clothing, or anything available.
  • Don't move spinal injury casualties: If the person is breathing and there's no immediate danger, keep them still until paramedics arrive.

Roadside Breakdown Safety

  • Get the bike off the road if possible
  • Put on your high-vis vest
  • Stand on the verge, away from traffic
  • Use your torch or phone light to be visible to passing vehicles
  • Call breakdown cover or 999 depending on the situation

Consider First Aid Training

The most important piece of emergency equipment is knowledge. Consider taking a first aid course before your tour — the Red Cross, St John Ambulance, and motorcycle-specific organisations like RoSPA offer courses specifically for motorcyclists. keyTakeaways: A proper first aid kit includes trauma dressings, conforming and triangular bandages, wound closures, gloves and painkillers, not just plasters.
Survival essentials: an emergency bivvy bag, whistle, head torch, fire-starting kit and hi-vis vest.
What3Words plus a charged phone and power bank cover location and communication.
At a scene: make it safe, call 999, do not remove helmets, control bleeding and keep the casualty warm.
Consider a first aid course such as Biker Down so you can actually use the kit.

faq.q: What should a motorcycle first aid kit contain?
faq.a: Go beyond plasters. Include trauma dressings and conforming bandages to control serious bleeding, a triangular bandage, adhesive wound closures such as Steri-Strips, antiseptic wipes, latex-free gloves, scissors and tweezers, painkillers and antihistamines. Motorcycle injuries can be significant, so a kit capable of managing a bleed is far more use than a basic plaster tin.

faq.q: What should I do first at the scene of an accident?
faq.a: Make the scene safe before anything else, protecting yourself and others from traffic. Call 999 and give your location, using What3Words if there is no road name. Do not remove a casualty's helmet unless they are not breathing and you must open the airway. Control any serious bleeding with direct pressure and keep the casualty warm and still.

faq.q: How do I stay warm if stranded overnight?
faq.a: Carry an emergency bivvy bag, which weighs around 100g and traps body heat, plus a fire-starting kit and a head torch. Put on all your layers, get off the cold ground, and use the bivvy bag to prevent heat loss. A whistle helps rescuers locate you, and a hi-vis vest makes you visible to passing vehicles and search teams.

faq.q: Is first aid training worth it for riders?
faq.a: Absolutely. Carrying a kit is only half the answer; knowing how to use it is what saves lives. Free courses such as Biker Down, run by fire and rescue services, teach scene management, helmet removal and bleeding control specifically for motorcyclists. A short course gives you the confidence to act effectively in the crucial minutes before an ambulance arrives.
